title: Data centers are becoming a local legitimacy problem as Americans connect AI infrastructure to energy, environment, and quality of life
source_unit: Pew Research Center survey analysis, Americans' views of data centers have turned more negative, September 2026
geography: United States; adults nationally with urban, suburban, rural, party, age, education, and awareness comparisons

denominator.unit: U.S. adults surveyed July 20-August 9, 2026 in Pew American Trends Panel

environment_mostly_bad.unit: percent saying data centers are mostly bad for the environment; 39% in January

home_energy_costs_mostly_bad.unit: percent saying data centers are mostly bad for home energy costs; 38% in January

nearby_quality_of_life_mostly_bad.unit: percent saying data centers are mostly bad for nearby quality of life; 30% in January

local_jobs_mostly_bad.unit: percent saying data centers are mostly bad for local jobs; 15% in January

local_tax_revenue_mostly_bad.unit: percent saying data centers are mostly bad for local tax revenue; 12% in January

observations.method: Pew Research Center American Trends Panel survey of 10,548 U.S. adults fielded July 20-August 9, 2026, compared with January 2026 responses.
observations.uncertainty: These are perceptions of possible effects, not measured electricity bills, emissions, jobs, tax receipts, or local quality-of-life outcomes; the shift does not establish which events or information changed opinion.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults nationally, with demographic, partisan, geographic, and awareness comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rising concern can reflect increased awareness and salience rather than realized local harm; people may oppose specific siting, rate allocation, water use, or governance arrangements rather than data centers in every form.

observations.period: August 2026; local comfort and community consent

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the July 20-August 9, 2026 survey

not_comfortable_local_data_center.unit: percent saying they would be not too or not at all comfortable with a new data center operating in their area

very_or_extremely_comfortable.unit: percent saying they would be extremely or very comfortable

somewhat_comfortable.unit: percent saying they would be somewhat comfortable

not_heard_of_data_centers.unit: percent saying they had not heard of data centers

democratic_discomfort.unit: percent of Democrats or Democratic leaners not too or not at all comfortable

republican_discomfort.unit: percent of Republicans or Republican leaners not too or not at all comfortable

observations.method: Pew descriptive comparison of comfort with a hypothetical new local data center, including party and place groups.
observations.uncertainty: Hypothetical comfort is not a vote, permitting decision, protest, or observed siting conflict; unfamiliarity and question framing may affect the response.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults by party, urbanicity, and awareness of data centers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Community resistance may be negotiable through local benefits, rate protections, water and land safeguards, transparency, or ownership arrangements; discomfort alone does not identify the preferred governance solution.

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the July 20-August 9, 2026 survey, with January comparison

heard_a_lot.unit: percent saying they had heard or read a lot about data centers; 25% in January

heard_at_least_a_little.unit: percent saying they had heard at least a little; 75% in January

heard_nothing.unit: percent saying they had heard nothing; 25% in January

observations.method: Pew repeated survey measure of public awareness alongside impact and comfort questions.
observations.uncertainty: Awareness is self-reported and does not measure factual understanding, exposure to a local project, or the quality of information received; increasing awareness may itself change the composition of opinion.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, with awareness varying by gender, education, and other groups reported by Pew.
observations.counterinterpretation: More awareness can increase opposition, support, or uncertainty depending on whether information emphasizes economic benefits, household costs, environmental burdens, or local control.

observations.period: January-August 2026; rural and partisan environmental concern

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Pew survey; subgroup comparisons use the relevant weighted group universes

rural_environment_bad.value: 50% in August, up from 32% in January
rural_environment_bad.unit: rural adults saying data centers are mostly bad for the environment

democrat_environment_bad.value: 62% in August, up from 50% in January

republican_environment_bad.value: 47% in August, up from 31% in January

rural_quality_of_life_bad.value: 45% in August, up from 28% in January
rural_quality_of_life_bad.unit: rural adults saying data centers are mostly bad for nearby quality of life

observations.method: Pew subgroup comparison across January and August 2026 survey waves, with rural, party, and age/education groups.
observations.uncertainty: Subgroup opinion changes do not establish local exposure or explain whether national political messaging, direct experience, or project siting drove the movement; the survey is not a map of planned facilities.
observations.subgroup: Rural adults, Democrats, Republicans, and other demographic groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cross-party and rural movement suggests the issue may be becoming a broad infrastructure-governance concern, but shared concern does not guarantee shared policy preferences or coalition action.

boundary: This record adds a local-legitimacy and household-cost layer to AI infrastructure: rising awareness is accompanied by more negative perceptions of environmental, energy, quality-of-life, jobs, and tax effects, plus broad discomfort with local siting. It does not establish realized impacts, causal opinion change, community decisions, rate effects, emissions, water use, or durable public consent.
